units.title: Livestock Production
units.intro:
Livestock = domesticated animals kept for food, work, fibre or income: cattle, sheep, goats, camels, donkeys, poultry (and a few others). Eritrea’s herd is mostly **extensive / pastoral–agro-pastoral** — animals walk to browse, with extra pressure in the dry season.

Book snapshot of national stock (order-of-magnitude): millions of sheep and goats, substantial cattle and camels, donkeys as the everyday transport animal, very few horses/mules, plus layers such as White Leghorn in more intensive pockets.

cards.title: 1.1.1 What livestock are
body: **Livestock** = any animal kept to produce **food, wool, skins or fur**, or to **work the land**. In Eritrea this means **cattle, sheep, goats, camels, pigs, poultry** and the **equines** (horses, mules and donkeys). Equines are kept mainly for **draught** (pulling) and **transport**.
**Animal production (animal husbandry)** is the practice of raising animals for products such as **meat, milk, eggs, honey** and even **fish** from ponds.

**A short history:** people began to domesticate animals more than **10 000 years ago**, starting with the **dog**. The first food animals were **ruminants** (cattle, sheep, goats), then pigs. Horses and cattle were also tamed for transport and draught.
**Why domestication mattered:**
- a **stable food supply**, so the human population could grow;
- **division of labour**: once food was secure, some people could become smiths, potters, traders or priests (a feature of civilisation);
- animals for **company, religious offerings** and **draught power**. In return the animals got protection and a regular food supply.

cards.title: How many animals does Eritrea have?
body: Goats are the most numerous: they survive on browse in the dry lowlands where cattle and sheep struggle.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Livestock status in Eritrea
body: Livestock matter in all **six zobas**. Most of Eritrea's animals are **indigenous** (local). The only exotic breeds found in large numbers are the **Holstein-Friesian** dairy cow and the **White Leghorn** layer hen. There are also several thousand **Large White** pigs.
Agriculture gives about **26 %** of Eritrea's GDP, and livestock give **15 % of that** agricultural share.
**Why output is still low:** most animals are kept in a **traditional, low-input** system. Three big constraints:
- **feed shortage**: too little feed, and of poor quality, especially in the dry season;
- **widespread diseases** and parasites;
- **unimproved breeds** with low milk and meat yields.
Animals also get little care in **feeding, health care and housing**, so Eritreans eat some of the lowest amounts of animal products per person in the world.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Types and classification of livestock
body: All farm animals belong to **Kingdom Animalia** and **Phylum Chordata**. They split at the **class**: poultry are **Aves** (feathers, eggs), the others are **Mammalia** (hair, suckle their young with milk).
Mammals are split into **orders by their hooves**:
- **Artiodactyla = EVEN-toed** (two hooves, a cloven hoof): cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and camels.
- **Perissodactyla = ODD-toed** (one hoof): horses, donkeys and mules.
They are split further into **families** by their digestive system:
- **Equines** are **hindgut fermenters**: microbes digest fibre in the **caecum and large intestine (colon)**.

- **Bovidae** (cattle, sheep, goats) and **Camelidae** are **foregut fermenters**: fibre is fermented in the fore-stomach (rumen) before the true stomach. Camels have a three-compartment stomach with no separate omasum, so they are called pseudo-ruminants.
- **Pigs and poultry** are **monogastric**, like humans.
**Two species of cattle:** *Bos taurus* = **humpless** (European breeds such as Holstein-Friesian); *Bos indicus* = **humped zebu** (Eritrea's Barka and Arado). They can interbreed.

cards.title: Correction: even-toed and odd-toed
body: The textbook says horses have an even number of toes and cattle, camels, goats and pigs an odd number. It is the **other way round**: **Artiodactyla** (artios = even) have **two** functional hooves; **Perissodactyla** (perissos = odd) have **one**. The order names in its Table 1.1 are right.
The textbook also says equines digest mainly in the caecum and the **small** intestine. Fibre fermentation in equines happens in the **caecum and the large intestine (colon)**.

cards.title: How a cow digests grass, step by step

steps.text: **Rumen** (80 % of an adult stomach): the cow swallows grass with little chewing. Bacteria, fungi and protozoa make the enzyme **cellulase** and ferment cellulose into energy (volatile fatty acids).

**Reticulum**: has a honeycomb wall. It sorts the food and sends boluses (**cud**) back up to the mouth. The cow ruminates up to **8 hours a day**. It also traps nails and wire, which can cause "hardware disease".
**Omasum** ("many leaves"): its leaves squeeze the food and absorb water and minerals.
**Abomasum = true stomach**: acid and enzymes digest the food (and the rumen microbes) as in a pig or a person.
Then the **small intestine**: most digestion and absorption. Order to remember: **R-R-O-A**.

cards.title: Correction: cellulase, not "cellulose"
body: The textbook says the microbes have "a digestive enzyme called **cellulose**". Cellulose is the plant fibre. The enzyme that breaks it down is **cellulase**. The cow cannot make cellulase itself; only its rumen microbes can.

cards.title: A calf's stomach grows up
body: In a newborn the abomasum is the largest part (60 %), because milk is digested there. When the calf starts eating grass, the rumen grows to 80 %.

cards.title: The newborn calf and colostrum
body: A newborn calf has an **undeveloped rumen** and lives on milk for the first weeks. When it suckles, a fold called the **oesophageal groove** closes and carries milk straight to the **abomasum**, past the rumen. Once the calf eats grass and hay, the rumen grows fast.
**Colostrum** = the first milk after calving. Give it **as soon as possible**, within the first hours, because:
- it is rich in **immunoglobulins** (antibodies). This is **passive immunity**: the calf receives ready-made antibodies from its mother;
- it is very **nutritious**: high in fat, protein and vitamins, but low in lactose;
- it is a **laxative**: it clears the first dung (meconium) from the gut.

cards.title: The pig: one stomach
body: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) → large intestine → anus.

cards.title: Digestion in pigs (monogastric)
body: Pigs have **one simple stomach**, like people (mono = one, gastric = stomach). They **cannot live on grass** and need grain and other low-fibre feeds.
- **Mouth:** teeth chew; saliva softens food and starts starch digestion.
- **Oesophagus:** muscle waves carry food down. The **cardiac valve** stops food coming back up.
- **Stomach:** hydrochloric acid and enzymes. Food leaves through the **pyloric valve**.
- **Duodenum:** **bile** (made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder) digests fat; **pancreatic juice** digests fat, starch and protein.
- **Jejunum and ileum:** most nutrients are absorbed here.
- **Caecum, large intestine and rectum:** water is absorbed and faeces form; they leave through the **anus**.

cards.title: The hen: crop and gizzard instead of teeth
body: Grit (small stones) in the gizzard does the job of teeth.

cards.title: Digestion in poultry
body: Poultry have a **short, simple tract**, and food passes through very fast.
- **Beak and tongue:** no chewing; food is swallowed whole.
- **Crop:** a stretchy pouch on the oesophagus that **stores** food.
- **Proventriculus:** the glandular stomach. It adds acid and **pepsinogen** (which becomes pepsin) to digest protein.
- **Gizzard:** a strong muscular stomach. With **grit** inside, it grinds grain. This is essential before proper digestion.
- **Small intestine:** bile and pancreatic enzymes; absorption.
- **Two caeca:** bacteria ferment leftovers. **Short colon:** absorbs water.
- **Cloaca:** faeces and urine mix and leave together, so hen droppings have a white cap of uric acid.

cards.title: 1.1.5 Breeding: improving the next generation
body: An animal's performance depends on its **environment** (feeding, health care, housing, management) **and** its **genetic make-up** (heredity). **Breeding** is the mating of a chosen male with a chosen female to get desired offspring.
In traditional herds mating is often **unplanned** (any bull serves any cow), so the herd does not improve. **Planned breeding** improves chosen traits.

**Tool 1: selection.** Keep the best animals of the breeds already in the country. Do this **first**, because (1) local animals vary a lot in milk, growth and fertility, and (2) local breeds are **adapted** to heat, disease and poor feed, and their genes must not be lost.

**Selection criteria depend on the purpose.** A dairy farmer keeps daughters of high-milk cows that calve regularly and have large udders. A traditional goat keeper looks at milk, litter size (twins), disease resistance, kid survival, and birth and weaning weights.
**Culling** = removing animals with undesirable traits: low milk, poor fertility, small kids or calves, frequent illness.

**Tool 2: cross-breeding.** Bring in the genes of a more productive breed, using an **exotic sire** or **artificial insemination (AI)** with the semen of a high-quality bull. The offspring are called **crosses**. It is a **drastic** step. It works only if the **environment is improved at the same time**: without better feed, health care and housing, the costs outweigh the gains.
Note: the textbook numbers this section "1.5", which is a printing slip. It belongs to 1.1.

cards.title: Worked example — why select males?
cards.problem: Activity 1.8: In selection, does choosing better males or better females bring faster change?

steps.text: A cow has about **one calf a year**. One bull (or AI semen) can sire **30–40 calves a year**, or thousands with AI.
So each good bull spreads his genes to far more offspring than any one cow.
Selecting the **male** therefore changes the herd much faster. Females are still culled for poor milk or fertility.

cards.answer: Selecting the male gives faster change, because one sire has many more offspring than one dam.

cards.title: Worked example — crossing without a better environment
cards.problem: Activity 1.9: What goes wrong if a farmer crosses his zebu cows with a Holstein bull but changes nothing else?

steps.text: The cross needs **more feed** to give more milk, but gets only dry-season straw, so it cannot reach its potential.
It has **less resistance** to heat, ticks and local diseases than the zebu, so more calves die and vet bills rise.
Result: higher costs, little extra milk, and the adapted local genes are diluted.

cards.answer: The crosses cannot express their potential and suffer more disease and heat stress, so the disadvantages outweigh the gains.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The chemical process of cellulose digestion in ruminants is achieved by enzymes produced by which of the following?
cards.why:
**Reasoning**
Ruminant animals do not naturally produce cellulase, the enzyme required to digest cellulose. Cellulase is produced by the symbiotic bacteria, protozoa, and fungi residing within the rumen and reticulum.

**Conclusion**
Thus, cellulose digestion is achieved by **Rumen microorganisms**.

cards.title: Feeds and feeding: the big picture
body: A **feed** is any material that an animal can eat, **digest, absorb and use**. "Feed" is used for animals and "food" for people, but they mean the same thing.
Part of what an animal eats is **not digested** and leaves as faeces. The parts that are digested and used are the **nutrients**.

In Eritrea the dry season is the hungry season: from about October to June animals live mainly on **straw, stover and browse**. Good feeding means giving **water first**, then enough energy and protein, plus salt and minerals.

cards.title: The six nutrients
body: Feed = water + dry matter. Dry matter = organic matter (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins) + inorganic matter (minerals, measured as ash).

cards.title: 1.2.1 Feed composition and the nutrients
body: **Six nutrients:** water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins and minerals.

**Dry matter (DM)** = everything except water (the other five nutrients). The DM is split into **organic matter** (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, which all contain carbon) and **inorganic matter** (the minerals, measured as **ash** after burning).
**Water** is the most urgent nutrient: animals die faster from lack of water than from lack of any other nutrient. Water:
- takes part in most body reactions (**hydrolysis**);
- is the **solvent** that carries nutrients and wastes;
- **controls body temperature**, because it makes up most of the body.
The water content of feeds varies widely: fresh alfalfa is about 65–80 % water, while straw and grain are only about 10 %.

cards.title: How much dry matter is in fresh alfalfa?
Worked example — dry matter (Activity 1.11)
cards.problem: Fresh alfalfa contains 65 % moisture. A farmer gives a cow 3 kg of fresh alfalfa a day. How much dry matter does the cow get?
cards.answer: 1.05 kg of dry matter per day.

cards.title: Carbohydrates: the energy feeds
body: Carbohydrates are the **main energy source** and the **largest part of every ration**. They contain C, H and O, with H and O in the same 2 : 1 ratio as in water.

- **Simple carbohydrates** (sugars and starch) are easily digested. Starch is stored in **grains and tubers** (sorghum, maize, barley, potato). Sugar-rich feeds are **molasses**, cane sugar and fruits.

- **Complex (structural, fibrous) carbohydrates**, mainly **cellulose** in plant cell walls, are hard to digest. Only the enzymes of **microbes** (in the rumen, or in the caecum of a horse or donkey) can break them down.
So a goat can live on straw and acacia leaves, but a hen cannot.

cards.title: Proteins and amino acids
body: Proteins contain **C, H, O and N**. **Nitrogen is found only in proteins** (among the main nutrients), so feed protein is estimated from its nitrogen content.
Proteins are long chains of **amino acids** (about 20 kinds). Digestion releases the single amino acids for absorption.
**Functions:** building blocks for **growth, milk, eggs and pregnancy**; **enzymes and hormones**; **repair** of tissues; **immunoglobulins** for body defence.

- **Essential amino acids** cannot be made in the body (or not fast enough), so **non-ruminants (pigs, poultry, people)** must get them from the feed. Example: lysine and methionine in a layer ration.
- **Non-essential amino acids** can be made in the body from other amino acids by **transamination** (moving an amino group).

- **Ruminants** do not need to worry about this: rumen microbes build all the amino acids from any nitrogen source, including **non-protein nitrogen (NPN)** such as **urea**. Non-ruminants cannot use NPN.

cards.title: Lipids (fats and oils)
body: Lipids contain C, H and O, like carbohydrates, but they give **2.25 times more energy** per kilogram. **Fats** are solid at room temperature; **oils** are liquid. They do not dissolve in water, only in organic solvents (ether, benzene, chloroform).
Oil-seed cakes (sesame, noug, groundnut) still contain some oil, which raises their energy value.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Sources and classes of feed
body: **Where feed comes from:** natural pasture; planted forages (**alfalfa, elephant grass**); crop residues (**straw** of barley, wheat and teff; **stover** of sorghum, maize and millet); by-products (wheat **bran** from mills, **molasses** from sugar, oil-seed **cakes**); and non-biological feeds such as **urea**.
**Concentrates vs roughages**, by fibre content:

- **Concentrates: fibre below 18 %.** They are dense, highly digestible and dry. **Energy-rich:** cereal grains. **Protein-rich:** oil-seed cakes. **Intermediate:** bran and middlings (less energy than grain, less protein than cake).
- **Roughages: fibre above 18 %.** They are bulky and less digestible, and only ruminants (and equines) use them well.

**Supplements** are small amounts added to improve the balance of the ration: protein (fishmeal, cake), energy (molasses), minerals (limestone for Ca, salt, bone meal) and vitamins (green leaves for vitamin A).
**Succulent vs dry:** fresh alfalfa or elephant grass cut and fed green is **succulent**. The same forage dried as **hay**, or straw and stover, is **dry** feed.

cards.title: Worked example — which carbohydrates only ruminants can use?
cards.problem: Activity 1.12: Name carbohydrate feeds that ruminants can get energy from but non-ruminants cannot.

steps.text: Non-ruminants have no microbes that make cellulase **before** the small intestine.
So feeds that are mostly **cellulose** are useful only to ruminants: **straw** (teff, barley, wheat), **stover** (sorghum, maize), **hay**, mature grass and browse.
Grain starch and molasses can be used by both.

cards.answer: Fibrous feeds (straw, stover, hay, mature grass, browse), which are rich in cellulose.

body: Cattle types by function: **beef, dairy, dual-purpose and multi-purpose**. Eritrea's local cattle are **multi-purpose** (draught, milk, meat, manure, savings). Holstein-Friesians are kept specially for milk around Asmara and other towns.

cards.title: Dairy cattle
body: Dairy breeds: **Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, Brown Swiss, Ayrshire** and Milking Shorthorn.

The **Holstein-Friesian** (black and white) was introduced by the Italians because the **cool highlands** suit it. It gives the **most milk and the most total butterfat** of any breed, although its fat % is lower than a Jersey's.

cards.title: Who is who on a dairy farm
Feeding dairy cows: roughage plus concentrate
body: **Roughage keeps the rumen healthy.** Chewing and ruminating fibre make a lot of **saliva**, which contains **bicarbonate buffers** that keep the rumen pH near neutral. A cow lying and chewing the cud is a healthy cow. Fibre also keeps the **butterfat %** of milk up: too little roughage gives low-fat milk and acid rumen problems.
**Concentrate is needed for high yields.** A cow can give about **5 L a day** from good roughage alone. For every **1.5 L above that**, give about **1 kg of concentrate**.

Eritrea is not yet self-sufficient in grain for people, so dairy farms use **agro-industrial by-products** that people do not eat: oil-seed cakes (sesame, noug, cotton seed), wheat bran and middlings, and molasses.

cards.title: Worked example — concentrate allowance
cards.problem: A Holstein cow at a farm near Asmara gives 14 L of milk a day on good alfalfa hay. How much concentrate should she get?

steps.text: Milk from roughage alone: about **5 L**.
Extra milk: 14 − 5 = **9 L**.
Concentrate: 9 ÷ 1.5 = **6 kg a day**, split between the two milkings.
Wash the udder with **warm water**. This cleans it and starts milk let-down (the hormone oxytocin).
Dry each teat with the cow's **own towel**, so mastitis germs do not pass between cows.
Squirt the first milk into a **strip cup**: clots or watery milk are signs of **mastitis**.
Milk **twice a day, about 12 hours apart**, by hand or machine.
**Dip the teats** in disinfectant to close out germs, then release the cow.

cards.title: Beef production and fattening
body: **Beef** = meat of mature cattle; **veal** = meat of calves. Beef breeds include **Angus, Hereford, Simmental, Charolais, Limousin, Gelbvieh, Brahman and Shorthorn**.

**Beef vs dairy type:** beef animals are **blocky**, shorter and well-muscled, with small udders, and turn feed into body weight. Dairy animals are **angular** (wedge-shaped) with large udders, and turn feed into milk.
**Intensive beef** is common where there is surplus grain; **extensive beef** on wide rangelands is slower to reach market weight.

**Fattening in Eritrea:** there is no specialised beef breed system. Instead, traders buy **thin adult animals** and feed them intensively for **4–6 months** near towns, using wheat bran, middlings, **sesame cake** and a little coarse grain. Gains are **0.6–1.2 kg a day**.

cards.title: Worked example — fattening gain
cards.problem: An ox bought at 260 kg is fattened for 150 days and gains 0.8 kg a day. What is its final weight?

steps.text: Final weight = 260 + 120 = **380 kg**.
Check: 150 days ≈ 5 months, inside the usual 4–6 months.

cards.title: Dehorning and castration
body: **Dehorning** removes the horns so animals cannot hurt each other or bruise the meat (bruised parts are cut off the carcass, or the whole carcass is condemned). Horned animals are also harder to handle. Do it in the **first two months** of life with a **dehorner**, a saw, an elastrator and rubber ring, or chemicals.

**Castration** removes the testes or makes them useless. It makes males **calmer and easier to handle**, stops unwanted mating, and stops male (secondary sex) characters developing. Castrated oxen are the usual ploughing animals.

- **Open castration:** a knife or scalpel cuts the bottom of the scrotum and the testes are removed (an emasculator may crush and cut the cord). It is sure, but the bleeding brings a risk of infection where flies are many.

- **Closed (bloodless) castration:** the **Burdizzo** crushes the spermatic cords through the skin, and the testes shrink (atrophy). An **elastrator** puts a tight **rubber ring** above the testes, which cuts off the blood so the scrotum dries and drops off. Closed methods suit the tropics, but are a little less certain than the open method.

body: **Poultry** = birds kept for human use that breed freely in captivity: chickens, ducks, turkeys, geese, guinea fowl, quails, pigeons and ostriches. A **broiler** is a young chicken raised for meat; the textbook's "broiler is the meat of poultry" is loosely worded.

cards.title: Small ruminants: sheep and goats
body: **Why smallholders like them:** they are cheap to buy and feed; they breed fast (twins are common); the loss is small if one dies; their milk is easily used or sold by the family; family labour (often children) can herd them; and they can be sold quickly for cash.

Their digestive system is like a cow's, but they **graze closer to the ground**. A sheep has a **split upper lip** for very short grass. Goats both **graze and browse**: their mobile upper lip and **bipedal stance** (standing on the hind legs) let them pick leaves between acacia thorns.
Tree leaves are **rich in protein**, so in the dry season lowland goats stay in better condition than sheep and cattle.

cards.title: Breeding and feeding goats
body: - A doe must **kid** before she gives milk; the kids are the second income.
- Usually **one kidding a year** in Eritrea; with good feeding, **three in two years**.
- **First mating by weight, not age:** at **three-quarters of the adult weight**. If she is mated too small, she keeps growing during pregnancy, so milk and kid growth suffer.
- A young **buck (billy goat)** can be fertile at **4 months** once both testes are in the scrotum. One buck serves **10–20 does**.
- **Heat signs** (every 17–21 days, lasting 24–36 h): tail wagging, bleating, restlessness, mounting other goats, a red, swollen vulva, and urinating in front of the buck.
- **Gestation: 145–150 days.** Stop milking **2 months** before kidding; give extra protein and minerals in the last **6 weeks**. **Wean** kids at **3 months**.
- **Water:** 3–8 L a day. **Protein:** young grass, leaves of **leucaena, sesbania and acacia**, legumes, cakes, bran. **Minerals:** salt, Ca and P. A goat that eats soil may be short of minerals.

cards.title: Worked example — when to mate a young doe
cards.problem: Adult local does in a village near Hagaz weigh about 28 kg. At what weight should a young doe be mated first?

steps.text: Rule: first mating at **¾ of adult weight**.
So weigh her (or use a weigh band) and mate her when she reaches about 21 kg, not at a fixed age.

cards.title: Beekeeping (apiculture)
body: Beekeeping produces **honey and wax**, and bees **pollinate** crops. A colony has **20 000–80 000** bees. The species: *Apis mellifera* (common honey bee), *A. dorsata* (giant), *A. laboriosa* (Himalayan giant), *A. cerana* (Indian) and *A. florea* (dwarf).

**Castes:** one **queen** (the fertile female, who lays all the eggs); thousands of **workers** (infertile females that build comb, collect nectar and pollen, make wax and honey, feed the young and guard the hive); and **drones** (males). Drones only mate with young queens and die after mating; they have **no sting**.
Bees communicate by **chemicals (smells) and dances** that show the direction and distance of food.
**Advantages:** little capital, little land of any quality, suits men and women of any age, can be a sideline or a business, and does not compete with crops or livestock for resources.
**Products:** honey, beeswax, pollen, **propolis** (bee glue from tree resins, used to seal cracks) and brood.

cards.title: 1.4 Why we house animals
body: - **Climate control:** protection from cold, heat, rain and draughts. In Eritrea most farmers bring all stock in at night, even where the climate is mild.
- **Control of breeding, health and feeding:** heat detection, mating and birth are easier to watch; diarrhoea and ticks are seen early; sick animals can be put in a **quarantine pen**.
- **Safety** from **theft** and predators such as **hyenas**.
- **Manure collection** for fertiliser or fuel.
There is no single design. A house must let animals **live, eat and rest comfortably**, and let the farmer **work easily**.

**Individual or group?** On a dairy farm keep milking cows, the bull, heifers and calves in **separate sections**: they are fed differently, the bull must not serve heifers that are too young, and the farmer must know which cow was mated. Calves are separated from their mothers soon after birth and fed from buckets. With only a few sheep or goats, **tethering** to a stake may be enough.

cards.title: Beef, sheep and goat housing
body: **Beef:** the simplest facilities. Cows can calve on pasture or in a lot near the farmstead; use open-fronted calving barns in the colder highlands. Keep separate lots for cows, heifers, bulls and calves. Every beef unit needs a **corral** with a **holding pen, working chute and head gate**, and good water.

**Sheep:** no costly building, just protection from severe cold. It must be **dry, draught-free and well ventilated**, with **0.1 m² of window per 2 m² of floor**, doors **2.4 m wide**, **1.1–1.4 m²** per ewe, **38–46 cm** of feeder space per ewe and **30.5 cm** per lamb.

**Dairy goats:** a small shed for a few goats; **loose pens** or **tie stalls** (often milking does in stalls, others loose). Confinement housing costs more but needs less bedding. House **bucks separately**.

cards.title: Worked example — planning a sheep house
cards.problem: A farmer near Adi Keyh plans a house for 40 ewes. Using 1.25 m² per ewe and 0.1 m² of window per 2 m² of floor, how much floor and window area does she need?

steps.text: Feeder space at 40 cm per ewe = 40 × 0.40 = **16 m** of trough.

cards.answer: 50 m² of floor, 2.5 m² of window and about 16 m of feeder.

cards.title: Poultry housing
body: Housing gives comfort and protection from weather and predators, and makes management easy. House **chicks, growers, layers, broilers and breeders separately**: they need different designs, and young birds catch diseases from older ones.
- **Width at most 9 m**, so air and light reach the middle; **length at most 30 m**.
- **Floor 30 cm above the ground**, to stop flooding and seepage; **concrete** is better than mud (easy to clean and disinfect, keeps rats out).
- **Nests:** the textbook recommends one nest per hen (many farms use one nest for every 4–5 hens), each about **35 cm deep × 30 cm wide × 35–40 cm high**, with a 20–22 cm entrance.

cards.title: Restraining animals
body: **Restraint** = controlling an animal so a job can be done safely (dosing, treating, milking). Approach calmly and confidently; never be harsh or hasty.
- **Nose ring** (iron) through the nasal septum, made with a nose punch; a rope on the ring controls a bull.
- **Bull holder:** a clamp with two half-rings that grips the septum when there is no ring.
- **Milkman's rope:** tied round both hind legs (with the tail) so the cow cannot kick or upset the pail.
- **Gags** keep the jaws apart for mouth checks, dosing or a stomach tube: **Drinkwater's gag** (aluminium, one for each side) or a wooden block with a hole and a strap.

cards.title: Step by step: Animal housing and equipment
body: **Step 1:** Purpose of housing: protect animals from weather (sun, rain, cold wind), predators and theft; make feeding, milking, disease control and record keeping easier.
**Step 2:** Choose the site: well-drained, slightly raised ground, near water and feed, easy to reach, away from homes downwind for smell.

**Step 3:** Good house requirements: enough space per animal, good ventilation and light, a sloping, easy-to-clean floor with drainage, a strong roof, and separate pens for young, sick or breeding animals.
**Step 4:** Equipment: feeders and water troughs, milking buckets and stools, dipping tank or spray for ticks, crush for handling, weighing scale, and cleaning tools.
**Step 5:** Keep it hygienic: remove dung daily, disinfect regularly, isolate sick animals, and provide clean bedding.

**Example:** A dairy farmer near Asmara builds a cow shed on a gentle slope with a concrete floor sloping to a drain, open sides with wire for ventilation, a feed trough along the front and a separate calf pen – cows stay clean, milk stays clean and mastitis is reduced.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "SPACE"
body: Site, Protection, Air (ventilation), Cleaning (drainage), Equipment.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: When asked to describe a good animal house, give each feature with its reason (e.g. "sloping floor – so urine and water drain away and the floor stays dry").

cards.q: Which hormone is responsible for milk let-down in dairy cows, stimulated by washing the udder with warm water?

Washing the udder with warm water sends sensory nerve impulses to the brain, triggering the pituitary gland to release oxytocin into the bloodstream. This hormone causes contraction of the alveoli, forcing milk down into the teats.

**Conclusion**
Thus, the milk let-down hormone is **Oxytocin**.

cards.title: 1.5 Signs of health
body: **Health** = the structure (anatomy) and functioning (physiology) that are normal for the species. Knowing the normal state lets you spot sickness early.
- **Appearance:** bright eyes; alert ears; a smooth, glossy coat with lick marks; loose skin that moves over the muscle; a **cool, moist muzzle**.
- **Behaviour:** normal posture, head up, walks freely, **stays with the herd**, and lies down and gets up easily.
- **Birds:** bright eyes; a smooth, glossy, **bright-red comb and wattles**; active, with the head held high and shiny feathers.
- **Digestion:** normal appetite and drinking, no foul breath, eager for green forage. **Feed left in the trough** is a warning.
- **Breathing:** easy and silent, moving both the chest and the belly.

body: Temperature is higher in **young** animals, often in **females**, in the **evening**, in late **pregnancy**, and after **exercise, fear or excitement**. So let the animal rest and handle it gently first.

cards.title: Taking the temperature (Activity 1.23)
body: Use a **clinical rectal thermometer** (35–44 °C). A narrow neck stops the mercury running back until you shake it down.

**Step 1:** shake the mercury down into the bulb. **Step 2:** grease the bulb with Vaseline. **Step 3:** lift the tail and insert the bulb gently into the rectum with a twisting movement, touching the wall. **Step 4:** wait **1 minute**, remove, wipe with cotton and read. **Step 5:** wash the thermometer in cold disinfectant (hot water would break it).
**Pulse:** count the beats for one minute. It is higher with exercise, excitement, fever or inflammation, and lower with anaemia and weakness.
**Breathing:** count the rise and fall of the flank (one rise + one fall = 1 breath), or feel the breath on your hand.

cards.title: Worked example — reading a temperature
cards.problem: A goat in Tesseney has a rectal temperature of 41.4 °C at 8 a.m. after resting in the shade. Is it sick?

steps.text: Normal goat range: **38.6–40.6 °C**.
41.4 is **0.8 °C above** the top of the range.
Morning temperatures are normally the lowest of the day, and the goat had rested, so exercise does not explain it.
Conclusion: **fever**. Isolate it and call the veterinary assistant.

cards.answer: Yes: 41.4 °C is a fever for a goat.

cards.title: Signs of sickness and what causes disease
body: **Disease** = any condition that upsets the normal working of the body (a lame cow is diseased). It can be **infectious** (caused by germs or parasites passed from another animal) or **non-infectious** (poisoning, injury, deficiency).

**Signs of a sick animal:** dull, depressed or restless; thin, with a rough coat and bare patches; poor appetite or **pica** (eating soil, bones or dung); diarrhoea and soiled tail; a staggering gait or lameness; pale, dark or bluish membranes; dry, cracked nostrils; noisy breathing; dark or bloody urine; and **standing apart from the herd**.
**Infection** = entry of a disease-causing micro-organism into the body.

**Micro-organisms:** **viruses** (the smallest; electron microscope only; live only inside cells); **bacteria** (single cells; some make toxins); **fungi** (spore-formers: moulds as threads, yeasts as single round cells); **protozoa** (single cells, often in blood and spread by ticks and biting flies).

cards.title: Zoonoses
body: A **zoonosis** is a disease that passes between animals and people. In this unit: **TB, brucellosis, anthrax and rabies**. FMD affects all **cloven-hoofed** animals (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs), but not horses or donkeys.

cards.title: Parasites
body: A **parasite** lives on or in another organism (the **host**) at the host's expense. The host of the adult stage is the **final (definitive) host**; the host of the larval stage is the **intermediate host**.
**Endoparasites** live inside: roundworms, tapeworms, flukes and protozoa. **Ectoparasites** live on the skin: ticks, mites, lice, fleas and flies.

**How they get in:** with food and water (roundworm eggs, fluke larvae); while grazing (tapeworm larvae in mites); through the skin (blood-fluke larvae); by contact (mange mites); or by the bite of ticks, flies and mosquitoes (protozoa).

**Harm they do:** steal food (worms); suck blood (hookworms, ticks); block the gut, bile ducts or blood vessels; make wounds through which germs enter; damage the liver and lungs; produce poisons; carry other germs (ticks carry babesia); and lower immunity.

cards.title: Ticks and babesiosis
body: **Babesiosis (piroplasmosis)** is a protozoan disease spread by **ticks**. Signs in cattle: high fever and **red urine** (haemoglobin from burst red blood cells), with anaemia.
**Tick control:**
- build an **acaricide channel** round the cattle shed so ticks cannot cross from the bush;
- treat **newly bought animals** with acaricide before they join the herd;
- clear the vegetation round sheds regularly;
- control **rodents**, which carry ticks;
- **dip, spray or dust** the animals regularly.

cards.title: 1.5.2 Preventing and controlling disease
body: **Prevention is cheaper than cure.** Well-fed, well-watered animals with shade or shelter, and not overworked, resist disease better. Adult animals often **carry** germs and parasites without signs (they became immune when young) and pass them to the young, so keep age groups apart.
Clean and disinfect utensils, harnesses and equipment regularly.
**During an outbreak:**
- **Isolation:** sick or suspected animals go to a separate place with their own attendant and utensils, until they can no longer spread infection.
- **Quarantine:** **apparently healthy** animals that may have been exposed, or **newly bought** animals, are kept apart for longer than the **incubation period** (for FMD about **14 days**).
- **Disinfection:** keep people and animals out; remove dung; scrub with **hot 4 % washing soda**; apply disinfectant and leave it for **24 hours**. Do not graze infected pastures; **lime** them.
- **Destruction and disposal:** kill animals that will not recover; **burn** the carcass or bury it **deep**.
- **Notification:** inform the Animal Health Department and the local people.
- **Immunisation:** vaccinate. It is the most effective method, but it does not replace the others.

steps.text: 1 : 1 000 means 1 g in 1 000 g, which is about 1 g per litre of water.
Dissolve 5 g in 5 L of clean water; it should be pale pink-purple.

cards.title: Immunity and vaccines
body: **Immunity** = the power to resist infection or toxins. Some animals are **naturally immune** to some diseases: dogs and cats to FMD and rinderpest, and fowl to anthrax. An animal that **recovers** from an infection is usually immune afterwards, because its body has made **antibodies**. Young animals get antibodies from **colostrum**, milk and their mother's blood.

**Vaccine:** contains the **antigen** (live, killed or weakened germs, or their products). The body responds by making its own antibodies, giving **active immunity** that lasts long but starts only after about **10–14 days**. Vaccinate **healthy** animals **before** an outbreak; vaccines prevent disease, they do not treat it.
- **Live attenuated** (weakened) vaccines give strong, long immunity from one dose.
- **Inactivated** (killed by heat, chemicals or radiation) vaccines are the safest, but give a weaker response and need repeat doses.
**Antiserum** (inoculation): serum with **ready-made antibodies**. It protects **at once**, which is useful in an outbreak, but only for a short time (**passive immunity**).

questions.q: A group of students in Keren is asked to classify the farm animals of Eritrea by the structure of their feet. Into which of the following Orders is a goat correctly placed?
why: **Recall the basis of the order-level division.** The unit states that mammals are divided into orders according to the structure of their feet.
**Identify the foot structure of a goat.** A goat has an even number of functional toes or hooves.
**Match the foot structure to the correct Order.** Animals with an even number of functional toes or hooves, such as cattle, sheep, goats, camels and pigs, belong to the Order Artiodactyla.

**Test each distractor.** Perissodactyla (odd number of toes: horses and donkeys) is wrong for a goat; Aves is the Class of birds, not a mammalian order; Equidae is the Family of the horse, not the order of a goat. Only Artiodactyla is correct.

questions.q: Using the same foot-structure rule, a donkey kept for transport in Massawa must be placed in which Order?

**Count the functional toes.** A donkey has an odd number of toes, so it is an odd-toed animal.
**Select the order.** Animals with an odd number of toes, such as horses and donkeys, belong to the Order Perissodactyla.

**Justify the distractors.** Artiodactyla covers even-toed animals (cattle, sheep, goats, camels, pigs); Equidae and Mammalia are the family of the horse and the class of all these mammals, not the order. The answer is B.

questions.q: During a practical lesson at an agricultural school near Asmara, students dissect the stomach of a mature cow and find that the abomasum (the true stomach) has a mass of $$154\text{ g}$$. The unit table gives the composition of the mature ruminant stomach as: rumen $$80\%$$, reticulum $$5\%$$, omasum $$7-8\%$$ and abomasum $$7-8\%$$. Taking the abomasum as $$7\%$$ of the total stomach, calculate the mass of the rumen.
why: **Identify the known and the unknown.** Known: mass of abomasum $$= 154\text{ g}$$, which is $$7\%$$ of the total stomach. Unknown: mass of the rumen, which is $$80\%$$ of the total stomach.
**State the percentage principle.** Part $$= \dfrac{\text{percentage}}{100} \times \text{whole}$$, so the mass of any compartment is its percentage share of the total stomach mass.
**Find the mass of the whole stomach.** Since $$7\%$$ of the total $$= 154\text{ g}$$, the total stomach mass $$= \dfrac{154 \times 100}{7} = 2200\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the mass of the rumen.** Mass of rumen $$= \dfrac{80}{100} \times 2200\text{ g} = 1760\text{ g}$$.

**Check the answer for reasonableness.** The rumen ($$1760\text{ g}$$) is much larger than the abomasum ($$154\text{ g}$$), which agrees with $$80\%$$ being far greater than $$7\%$$. The rumen mass is $$1760\text{ g}$$ ($$1.76\text{ kg}$$).
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A student at a livestock training centre in Keren works out that the abomasum of a mature goat makes up $$8\%$$ of the total stomach and has a mass of $$120\text{ g}$$. Using the unit's mature-animal figures (rumen $$80\%$$, reticulum $$5\%$$), find the mass of the rumen.
why: **Set out the percentages.** Abomasum $$= 8\%$$ of the total stomach and has a mass of $$120\text{ g}$$; rumen $$= 80\%$$ of the total stomach.
**Apply the percentage principle.** Part $$= \dfrac{\text{percentage}}{100} \times \text{whole}$$, therefore whole $$= \dfrac{\text{part} \times 100}{\text{percentage}}$$.
**Compute the total stomach mass.** Total $$= \dfrac{120 \times 100}{8} = 1500\text{ g}$$.
**Compute the rumen mass.** Mass of rumen $$= \dfrac{80}{100} \times 1500\text{ g} = 1200\text{ g} = 1.2\text{ kg}$$.
**State the result.** The rumen of the goat has a mass of $$1200\text{ g}$$ ($$1.2\text{ kg}$$), which is ten times the abomasum as expected from $$80\%$$ against $$8\%$$.
questions.tip: Write your answer first, then open the worked solution and compare the key facts and numbers.

questions.q: A dairy farm assistant at a milk collection centre in Asmara records the reticulum of a mature cow as $$75\text{ g}$$. In the mature animal the reticulum forms $$5\%$$ and the abomasum $$7\%$$ of the total stomach. Calculate the mass of the abomasum of the same cow.
why: **Identify the known and the unknown.** Known: reticulum $$= 75\text{ g} = 5\%$$ of the total stomach. Unknown: abomasum, which is $$7\%$$ of the total stomach.
**State the percentage principle.** Because each compartment's mass comes from the same total stomach, the masses are in the same ratio as the percentages.
**Find the total stomach mass.** Total $$= \dfrac{75 \times 100}{5} = 1500\text{ g}$$.
**Calculate the abomasum mass.** Mass of abomasum $$= \dfrac{7}{100} \times 1500\text{ g} = 105\text{ g}$$.
**Check and conclude.** Since $$7\% > 5\%$$, the abomasum ($$105\text{ g}$$) is heavier than the reticulum ($$75\text{ g}$$), which is consistent. The abomasum has a mass of $$105\text{ g}$$.

questions.q: A development agent in the hot, arid lowlands of the Northern Red Sea zone advises a livestock owner to keep humped Zebu cattle rather than imported temperate cattle, while expressing a preference for exotic dairy breeds only in the cool highlands near Asmara. Using the unit's account of the two cattle species and of indigenous versus exotic breeds, explain the biological and management reasons behind this advice.
questions.answer: Zebu cattle (Bos indicus) are humped, heat-tolerant and highly resistant to tropical diseases, so they suit the hot, arid lowlands, where they match the indigenous breeds already kept in Eritrea; temperate Bos taurus and exotic dairy breeds such as Holstein-Friesian have been introduced only to raise production in specific areas such as the cool Asmara highlands, because feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to each animal's biological needs.
why: **State the two cattle species and their characteristics.** The unit explains that cattle are divided into two main species: Bos taurus, which is humpless and adapted to cool, temperate climates, and Bos indicus, the humped Zebu cattle, which are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases.

**Link the species characters to the lowland environment.** The hot, arid lowlands impose high temperatures and a heavy burden of tropical disease, so the Zebu's heat tolerance and disease resistance make it the better biological match than the heat-sensitive, disease-susceptible Bos taurus.

**Bring in the indigenous breeds of Eritrea.** The unit states that most of Eritrea's livestock are indigenous (local) breeds, which means they are already established and suited to the local feed, climate and disease conditions of the country.

**Explain the role of exotic breeds.** Exotic breeds such as Holstein-Friesian dairy cattle have been introduced in specific areas to increase production, so they are useful where management and climate allow higher output rather than survival alone.

**Justify the highland recommendation.** The cool highlands around Asmara resemble the temperate conditions to which Bos taurus and Holstein-Friesian cattle are adapted, so the exotic dairy breed can express its production potential there with less heat and disease stress.

**Conclude with a management principle.** The unit notes that animal feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to the biological needs of each class and order, so breed choice must follow the environment and the intended purpose: hardy Zebu for survival and work in the lowlands, and exotic dairy stock for high production where conditions are favourable.

questions.q: A farmer in the lowlands of Eritrea can keep only animals that tolerate heat and resist tropical disease, while a neighbour in the cool highlands wants the highest possible milk yield. Using the unit's distinction between indigenous and exotic breeds, explain what each farmer should keep and why.
questions.answer: The lowland farmer should keep indigenous cattle such as the humped Zebu (Bos indicus), which are resistant to heat and tropical diseases and already adapted to local conditions, while the highland farmer may keep an exotic dairy breed such as the Holstein-Friesian, which has been introduced specifically to increase production and performs best where the climate is cool.
why: **Recall the indigenous-breed advantage.** Most livestock in Eritrea are indigenous (local) breeds, adapted to the country's climate, feed and disease challenge.
**Identify the lowland animal.** For heat and tropical disease, the unit points to Bos indicus (Zebu), the humped cattle that are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases.
**Recall the exotic-breed purpose.** Exotic breeds such as the Holstein-Friesian dairy cow have been introduced in specific areas of Eritrea to increase production.

**Match breed to environment and purpose.** The lowland farmer needs survival and adaptability, so indigenous Zebu is appropriate; the highland farmer has temperate-like conditions and a production objective, so the exotic dairy breed is appropriate.
**Conclude with the general rule.** Feed, housing and healthcare must be customized to the biological needs of the animal, so breed choice must match both the environment and the production goal.

questions.q: A cooperative near Massawa wants to introduce Holstein-Friesian cows alongside its local Zebu herd, and also plans to keep poultry. Explain, using the unit's ideas of adaptation and of exotic breeds, the risks of the plan and the single management measure the unit recommends for newly purchased animals.
questions.answer: The Holstein-Friesian is an exotic dairy breed adapted to cooler conditions, so in the hot lowlands near Massawa it is exposed to heat and tropical disease stress that the local Zebu resists; the unit's recommended safeguard for newly purchased animals is quarantine, the temporary isolation of the new animals for usually $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ to ensure they are not carrying hidden infections before they join the herd.
why: **Recall the nature of the exotic breed.** The Holstein-Friesian is described as an exotic dairy breed introduced in specific areas to increase production, not as a heat- and disease-resistant local breed.
**Compare with the local Zebu.** Bos indicus (Zebu) cattle are highly resistant to heat and tropical diseases, whereas Bos taurus cattle are adapted to cool, temperate climates.

**Deduce the risk near Massawa.** In the hot lowlands the imported Holstein-Friesian would face heat and tropical disease stress that the resident Zebu tolerates, so production and survival may be poor.
**Recall the safeguard for new stock.** The unit states that quarantine is the temporary isolation of newly purchased animals for usually $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ to detect hidden infections.

**State the recommendation.** The cooperative should quarantine the newly purchased cattle for $$14\text{ to }30\text{ days}$$ before mixing them with the local herd, and should expect that the exotic breed needs housing, feed and healthcare customized to its biological needs.

questions.answer: A foregut fermenter (cow, sheep, goat, camel) ferments fibre in the fore-stomach (rumen) before the true stomach; a hindgut fermenter (horse, donkey) ferments it in the caecum and large intestine after the small intestine.
why: Step 1: Both depend on microbes to digest cellulose.
Step 2: The difference is where: before (rumen) or after (caecum/colon) the small intestine.
Step 3: Ruminants can also digest the microbes themselves in the abomasum, so they gain more protein.
questions.tip: Fore = front = rumen; hind = back = caecum.

similar.q: Is a pig a foregut or a hindgut fermenter?
similar.a: Neither in a big way: it is monogastric and digests little fibre.

questions.answer: It gives antibodies (immunoglobulins) for passive immunity; it is very nutritious (high protein, fat and vitamins); and it is a laxative that clears the first dung.

questions.q: Why can a goat live on straw and browse while a pig cannot?

Step 2: Only microbial enzymes break cellulose.
Step 3: The goat has them in the rumen; the pig does not.
